statement: As described second-hand in one historical narrative review (Passie, 2018), whose estimates rest on a sparse literature and on information given to the author, a few dozen therapists in the United States, most in California and elsewhere on the West Coast, used MDMA in psychotherapy from the late 1970s until it was scheduled in 1985, while it was neither an approved medicine nor a controlled substance. The caseloads reported come mostly from the practitioners' own accounts, among them more than 80 patients treated by Greer and Tolbert from 1980 to 1985. The outcome evidence the review describes consists of practitioners' reports, a 1984 exploratory survey of 16 therapists, an unpublished 1980 study in which nine people had one MDMA session each, and a follow-up of 29 of Greer and Tolbert's patients, which found no serious side effects. Two therapists had sexual contact with patients during MDMA sessions; both were sued and lost their licences. After the DEA recommended placing MDMA in Schedule I in July 1984, its administrative law judge concluded at the 1985 hearings that this was not required, and the DEA overruled the judge; the WHO's expert committee, when MDMA was scheduled internationally in late 1985, judged the therapeutic reports methodologically inadequate but urged research. Five applications to study MDMA submitted from 1986 to 1988 were put on clinical hold, and the first FDA-approved study of MDMA in humans, in healthy volunteers, began in 1992. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Before it was banned in 1985, a few dozen therapists in the United States used MDMA in talking therapy. Their reports were positive, but experts for the World Health Organization judged them not well enough designed to rely on, and two therapists had sex with patients during sessions. A US judge advised against the strictest ban, but the drug agency imposed it anyway. This history comes from one review based on old reports, memoirs and the author's own contacts.
population: Patients of psychotherapists in the United States who used MDMA before it was scheduled (late 1970s to 1985)
exposure: MDMA used in individual, couples and group psychotherapy
outcome: Extent and nature of therapeutic use; outcome evidence of the period; documented misconduct; scheduling sequence
magnitude: A few dozen therapists, 1977 or 1978 to 1985; reported caseloads: Zeff about 4000 people over 12 years (from a memoir), Greer and Tolbert more than 80 patients (1980 to 1985), Ingrasci 100 patients in about 150 sessions, Harlow more than 200 clients; outcome reports: Greer and Tolbert follow-up of 29 (23 with positive changes lasting 1 week to 2 years, no serious side effects), ARUPA survey 15 of 16 therapists positive; two therapists lost their licences after sexual contact with patients during sessions; DEA recommended Schedule I on 27 July 1984, its judge concluded against in 1985, overruled; five research applications on clinical hold (1986 to 1988); first FDA-approved human study 1992.

evidence.extracted: From the relatively poor data in the literature and information given personally to the author, a few dozen therapists, most in California and elsewhere on the West Coast, used MDMA in psychotherapy between 1977 (title and abstract) or 1978 (Discussion) and 1985, when it was neither an FDA-approved drug nor a controlled substance; a physician could use it legally if self-synthesized, with informed consent and a peer-reviewed protocol.

evidence.locator: George Greer's work with MDMA in psychotherapy, 1st and 5th paragraphs; Leo Zeff—The Secret Chief, 2nd paragraph; Rick Ingrasci: MDMA in couples and patients with life-threatening illnesses, 1st paragraph; A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Greer, a psychiatrist, and Tolbert, a psychiatric nurse, treated more than 80 patients from 1980 to 1985; their published follow-up of 29 patients found no serious side effects or negative after-effects and 23 with positive changes lasting from 1 week to 2 years; Zeff gave MDMA to about 4000 people over 12 years (from a memoir); Ingrasci treated 100 patients in about 150 sessions, one-third with couples; Harlow treated more than 200 clients before 1985.

evidence.locator: A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Kueny's 1980 study, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: A 1984 exploratory survey of 16 therapists for ARUPA: 15 judged MDMA valuable in augmenting psychotherapy and all claimed complications were negligible; it was used as evidence at the hearings; an unpublished 1980 study gave one MDMA session to each of nine people.

evidence.locator: Physical abuse in MDMA-assisted psychotherapy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Two therapists, Rick Ingrasci and Francesco DiLeo, initiated intimate body contact, sexual touch and intercourse with patients during MDMA sessions; both were sued and lost their licences; a Maryland appeals court (1991) upheld damages to DiLeo's patient, later diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety.

evidence.locator: Therapists opposed to the scheduling of MDMA in 1985, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th, 6th and 8th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The DEA recommended Schedule I on 27 July 1984; at the 1985 hearings its administrative law judge concluded that MDMA did not have to be placed in Schedule I; the DEA overruled the judge's decision; the WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, which scheduled MDMA internationally in late 1985, found the therapeutic reports intriguing but methodologically inadequate and urged research; five applications to study MDMA submitted from 1986 to 1988 were placed on clinical hold; after the FDA rejected a patient study and recommended a study in healthy volunteers, the first FDA-approved MDMA study in humans began in 1992.

risk_of_bias.note: One narrative review by a single author, relaying memoirs, interviews and proponents' documents without appraisal; the figures are second-hand.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive historical claim (starts low), resting only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3: stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand), rated down once because the review relays unappraised sources. It describes the period; it makes no claim that MDMA-assisted therapy worked or was safe then. The primary documents of 1986 on the list (Greer and Tolbert; Downing; Grinspoon and Bakalar) should replace these anchors when saved.
